title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 236
paragraphs: After him spoke Achaimenes, Xerxes's brother and also commander of the fleet, who happened to be present at this conversation and was afraid that Xerxes might be persuaded to do this. “O king,” he said, “I see that you are listening to the words of a man who envies your good fortune — or who is even a traitor to your cause. For truly the Greeks delight in that very temper; they envy a man for his good luck, and they hate whatever is stronger than themselves. If, on top of the other misfortunes we have suffered — since four hundred of our ships have been wrecked — you now send off another three hundred from the fleet's station to sail around the Peloponnese, then your opponents become a match for you in battle; whereas while the fleet is all assembled together it is hard for them to deal with, and they will not be a match for you at all. Moreover, the whole naval force will support the land force and be supported by it, if they go forward together; but if you divide them, neither will you be of use to them nor they to you. My determination is rather to put your own affairs in good order and not to concern yourself with the affairs of the enemy — where they will mount the war, or what they will do, or how many they are. It is enough that they take thought for themselves, and we likewise for ourselves. And if the Lacedaemonians come out to fight the Persians, they will certainly not heal the wound from which they are now suffering.”
